answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1925–2012 · American novelist, essayist and public intellectual
answer.sourceLine: The saying is Gore Vidal’s, and he said so himself. Asked about it on the Charlie Rose show on 31 December 2009, he replied: “I said that to Diane Sawyer.” The earliest documented appearance in print is older — Lewis H. Lapham’s column “The Easy Chair: The American Courtier” in Harper’s for October 1978, page 17 — and it credits Vidal there too. Quote Investigator ↗ finds “good evidence that Gore Vidal employed this adage during the 1970s” while cautioning that “the phrasing is highly variable.”
answer.confidenceText: Attributed — Vidal claimed it on air, but it is a spoken quip and the wording has never settled.

source.excerpt: Never miss a chance to have sex or appear on television.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ gives the earliest citation as Lewis H. Lapham’s column “The Easy Chair: The American Courtier” in Harper’s, October 1978, page 17 — where the adage is already credited to Gore Vidal, not claimed by Lapham.

Its conclusion: “there is good evidence that Gore Vidal employed this adage during the 1970s, and he has directly taken credit for the coinage. The phrasing is highly variable.” The credit-taking is on the record — QI reproduces the exchange from the Charlie Rose show of 31 December 2009, in which Rose asks about the line and Vidal answers, “I said that to Diane Sawyer.”

The chronology QI assembles runs through the Washington Post in 1982, Bob Chieger’s Was It Good for You, Too? in 1983 (page 238), Lapham again in the Baltimore Sun in 1985, Michael Kinsley in the Washington Post in 1988, and the Oxford Dictionary of Humorous Quotations in 2008 (page 319) — Vidal named throughout.

We read Wikiquote’s Gore Vidal page ↗ in full. It carries the line in its sourced quotes, not in its Misattributed section — but in the form “Never pass up a chance to have sex or appear on television,” cited to the same 1983 Chieger book from which QI quotes “never miss.” Two careful sources, one book, two wordings: that is what QI means by highly variable.

Dates checked independently: Gore Vidal, 3 October 1925 – 31 July 2012 ↗, and Lewis H. Lapham, 8 January 1935 – 23 July 2024 ↗, who edited Harper’s from 1976 to 1981 — which is where the October 1978 column sits.
source.excerptNote: Vidal appears never to have written the line down. It reaches us through other people’s reporting of his talk — Lapham in Harper’s in 1978, then a run of newspapers and quotation books through the 1980s. Vidal’s own account, given to Charlie Rose in 2009, is that he said it to Diane Sawyer. We could not consult the 1978 issue of Harper’s ourselves; the wording and the page locator come from Quote Investigator ↗

The earliest text carrying the wording is Lapham’s Harper’s column of October 1978, and every later source QI cites is later still, so the printed forms are in copyright. Quoting the one-line adage with attribution is ordinary quotation; reproducing Lapham’s column is not.

author.heading: About Gore Vidal
author.metaLine: 1925–2012 · American novelist, essayist and public intellectual
author.bio: Gore Vidal (1925–2012), born Eugene Louis Vidal, was an American writer and public intellectual known for his cynical, epigrammatic wit. His novels and essays attacked the social and sexual norms he saw driving American life, and he ran twice, unsuccessfully, as a Democratic candidate — for the House in 1960 and the Senate in 1982. A grandson of Senator Thomas Gore, he spent much of his career on television, which is the joke this line is making.

copyAttribution: "Never miss a chance to have sex or appear on television." — Gore Vidal. Earliest documented in Lewis H. Lapham, "The Easy Chair: The American Courtier," Harper's, October 1978, page 17, where it is already credited to Vidal. Vidal confirmed it on the Charlie Rose show, 31 December 2009. misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who only carried it
misattribution.intro: This quotation is unusual: the man whose name sits on the earliest printed source never claimed it, and the man who did claim it left nothing in writing.

items.why: Lapham printed the line first, in Harper’s in October 1978, and returned to it in the Baltimore Sun in 1985. But he credited Vidal on both occasions, and Quote Investigator ↗ nowhere suggests he coined it. Being the earliest source for a saying is not the same as being its author — the confusion is what put his name on this page.

Both forms are everywhere, and a first-person variant (“I never miss a chance…”) circulates too. Wikiquote prints the “pass up” form ↗ citing Bob Chieger’s Was It Good for You, Too? (1983), while QI quotes “never miss” from page 238 of the same book. QI’s verdict on the whole family is short: “The phrasing is highly variable.”

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: Gore Vidal, spoken — earliest in print in Lewis H. Lapham, “The Easy Chair: The American Courtier,” Harper’s, October 1978, page 17, and confirmed by Vidal himself on the Charlie Rose show in December 2009 ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line belongs to a moment when American writers were working out that television was a place to be somebody rather than a distraction from the writing. Vidal, who spent a great deal of his career on air, is telling the joke about himself as much as about anyone else.

It has since become a stock line about media vanity, quoted at people who chase the camera. Quote Investigator ends its own piece with the driest possible note on that: “it is not clear how closely Vidal has followed his own advice.”
context.pull: “I said that to Diane Sawyer.” — Gore Vidal, asked on television whether he had said it.

QI's earliest citation is Lewis H. Lapham, 'The Easy Chair: The American Courtier', Harper's, October 1978, page 17, where the adage is credited to Gore Vidal.
QI reproduces an exchange from the Charlie Rose Television Show of 31 December 2009 in which Rose asks about the saying and Vidal answers 'I said that to Diane Sawyer.'

QI's chronology after 1978 runs: Washington Post 1982 (Henry Allen), Dream Jobs 1983, Bob Chieger's Was It Good for You, Too? 1983 page 238, Baltimore Sun 1985 (Lapham), Washington Post 1988 (Michael Kinsley), Oxford Dictionary of Humorous Quotations 2008 page 319. QI never attributes the coinage to Lapham.

Wikiquote's Gore Vidal page lists 'Never pass up a chance to have sex or appear on television.' among his sourced quotes, cited to Bob Chieger, Was It Good For You, Too? (1983); it is not in the page's Misattributed section.

Gore Vidal, born Eugene Louis Vidal, lived 3 October 1925 to 31 July 2012 and was an American writer and public intellectual known for his cynical epigrammatic wit; he ran unsuccessfully as a Democrat for the House in 1960 and the Senate in 1982, and was a grandson of Senator Thomas Gore.
Lewis Henry Lapham II (8 January 1935 - 23 July 2024) edited Harper's Magazine from 1976 to 1981 and from 1983 to 2006.
